Borrowed from Medieval Latin Francigena, from Francia + -gena. By surface analysis, Francia + -geno.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin frāternālis (“fraternal”), from Latin frāternus (“of or pertaining to a brother, fraternal”), from frāter (“brother”).
From Medieval Latin frigium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin phrenesia, from Latin phrenēsis, from Ancient Greek φρένησις (phrénēsis), derived from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin frontālis, from Latin frontem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin fungibilis, derived from Latin fungor.
From Medieval Latin fustaneum, from fustis.
From Medieval Latin, Latinized form of Frankish *wala (“good, well”), from Proto-Germanic *wal-, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose, wish”).
From Medieval Latin galeria (“gallery”), perhaps an alteration of galilea (“church porch”), probably from Latin Galilaea (“Galilee”), region of Israel. More at Galilee.

parole.significato: a feudal vassal of the king in the time of the Lombards
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin gasindus, from Lombardic and Old High German gisindi, from Proto-West Germanic *gasinþ, from Proto-Germanic *gasinþô (“comrade, companion”).
From Medieval Latin castaldus, gastaldus (“manager”, “bailiff”, “steward”), from Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌻𐌳𐍃 (*gastalds, “occupying”, “administering”, occurring in compound words), from 𐌲𐌰𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌻𐌳𐌰𐌽 (gastaldan).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin geōrgiānus. By surface analysis, Georgia + -iano.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin hierarcha, from Ancient Greek ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs, “high priest”).
From Medieval Latin jacintus, from Latin hyacinthus, from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos, “any of several dark blue flowers; a blue precious stone”).

parole.significato: a neighborhood in any of several Italian cities once reserved to the Jews; a ghetto
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin iudeca, from Latin iūdaica, feminine form of iūdaicus (“Judaic, Jewish”), ultimately from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (y'hudá, “Judah”). Doublet of giudaica. Compare Sicilian judeca.

parole.significato: the office of a judge; judgeship
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin iūdicātūra (“judgeship”). By surface analysis, giudicato (“judgement”) + -ura (collective suffix).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Scientific Latin iugularis, jugularis, from Latin iugulum.
From Medieval Latin iūrista.
Variant of nuca (“nape”), from Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ, “bone marrow”).

parole.significato: a unit of measure of length, equivalent to 0.7442 m
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin goa.
From Medieval Latin gualdus, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *walþuz.
From Medieval Latin waraniō, warangio, borrowed from Frankish *wrainijō (“stallion”), from Proto-Germanic *wrainijô.

parole.significato: a foreigner with limited legal capacity granted by royal protection
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin guaregangus, wargengus, warengangus, of Germanic origin.
From Medieval Latin werigeldum, weregildum, wergeldus, from Proto-West Germanic *werageld.
From Medieval Latin īconoclasta, from Ancient Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs, “breaker of images”).
From Medieval Latin īdenticus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin illēgālis, from Latin lēgālis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin imponderābilis.
From Medieval Latin importantia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin incēnsāre (“to perfume with incense”), from Latin incēnsus (“incense”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin incīsīvus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inclūsīvus, from Latin inclūsus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin incorruptibilitātem.

parole.significato: to charge (with), to accuse, to indict
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incrīmināre, from Latin crīmnāre.

parole.significato: to invalidate, reduce in validity or value
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin īnficior, alteration of Classical Latin īnfitior (“to deny, contradict”), from *īnfitiae (“denial”) (see īnfitiās eō), from fateor (“to admit, acknowledge”).
From Medieval Latin īnstallāre (“to install, put in place, establish”), from in- + stallum (“stall”), from Frankish *stall (“stall, position, place”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intangibilis, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tangō. By surface analysis, in- + tangibile.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin integrālis, from Latin integer.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intēnsīvus, from Latin intēnsus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intertenēre, derived from Classical Latin tenēre (“to hold; to possess”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intoxicāre, from Latin toxicāre, verb based on Latin toxicum (“poison”). By surface analysis, in- + tossico (“poison”) + -are (1st conjugation verbal suffix).

parole.significato: to insert (something, e.g. a clause into a contract), to slip in (stealthily or by force)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin intrūdere, from in- + trūdō.
From Medieval Latin intuitiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inventivus, from Latin inventum.
From Medieval Latin irresistibilis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin īnstantāneus, from Latin īnstantem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin labiālis (“of the lips”), derived from Latin labium (“lip”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *leb- (“to hang loosely”).

From labiale (“labial”) + -izzare, from Medieval Latin labiālis (“of the lips”), derived from Latin labium (“lip”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *leb- (“to hang loosely”). By surface analysis, labial(e) (“labial”) + -izzare (“-ize”, verbal derivational suffix).
From Medieval Latin lacca, of Arabic لَكّ (lakk), from Persian لاک (lâk), from Hindi लाख (lākh), from Sanskrit लाक्षा (lākṣā).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin lagnum, from Vulgar Latin *lanium, of Mediterranean substrate origin; compare Clanius, Clanis, names of rivers.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin lampreda, of uncertain origin: possibly from Late Latin lampetra, from a combination of Latin lambere (“to lick”) + petra (“stone”). Compare Spanish lamprea, French lamproie, Portuguese lampreia. However see also Gaulish naupreda.
From Medieval Latin astracum, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “shell, sherd”). Perhaps related to lastra.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin; perhaps from Latin līvidus (“bluish”) and influenced by lavanda (“washing”).

parole.significato: a lazar house or leper colony
parole.testo: From lazzaro (“lazar, leper”) + -etto (“-ette: forming diminutives”), from Medieval Latin lazarus (“leper”), an antonomasia from Lazarus, from Koine Greek Λᾱ́ζᾱρος (Lā́zāros), the given name of the Biblical character found in Luke 16, from Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר (“Eleazar”, literally “God has helped”), a

From Medieval Latin lazarus (“leper”), an antonomasia from Lazarus, from Koine Greek Λᾱ́ζᾱρος (Lā́zāros), the given name of the Biblical character found in Luke 16, from Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר (“Eleazar”, literally “God has helped”), a given name shared by various figures in the Hebrew Bible.
From legittimo + -are, or borrowed from Medieval Latin lēgitimāre, from Latin legitimus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin licentiāre. Compare French licencier.
From Medieval Latin linguālis, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech”).

parole.significato: flax mill, linen mill, linen factory
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin linificium. By surface analysis, lino + -ificio.
From liscivia + -are or borrowed from a Medieval Latin lixiviāre.
From Medieval Latin, Late Latin laudum, from Latin laudō.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin logotheta, borrowed from Byzantine Greek λογοθέτης (logothétēs), from Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos) + θέτης (thétēs).

parole.significato: that ripens in July (of fruit etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Medieval Latin iūliāticus, lūliāticus. By surface analysis, luglio + -atico. Compare Emilian aliadgh, liadga, Romagnol agliêdga.
From Medieval Latin macis, corrupted from Latin macir.
From Medieval Latin maiorana
Borrowed from Medieval Latin magnesia.
Derived from Medieval Latin maiestāticus, derived from Classical Latin maiestās.
Alteration of Medieval Latin magnēsia.

parole.significato: an amount of land (usually 12 jugerums) considered cultivable yearly by using two oxen or a single plough
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin mānsum (“residence”), from Latin mānsus, perfect passive participle of maneō (“to stay, remain”).
From Medieval Latin manutentiōnem, form of manutentiō, derived from Latin manū tenēre.
From Medieval Latin mappa mundī (literally “chart of the world”).
From Medieval Latin mergō, mergōnem, from Latin mergus (cf. smergo, Portuguese mergulhão, Spanish somorgujo, Sicilian maraguni). Also cognate with Venetan marangon and Romansh marangun (“carpenter”).

From Medieval Latin marchionissa, feminine form of marchion, from Late Latin marcha, from Frankish *markōn (“to mark, mark out, to press with the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *markō (“area, region, edge, rim, border”). Cognate with Sicilian marchisa.
From Medieval Latin marca, similar to Old French marc.

parole.significato: sort of farmstead typical of South Tyrol
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mānsum. Compare Catalan mas (“farmhouse”).
From Medieval Latin *massārius, from Latin massa.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin māternitātem.

parole.significato: by, through, by means of, using
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin mediante, from the ablative singular of Late Latin mediantem, present active participle of mediō (“to be in the middle”).
From Medieval Latin medicālis, from Latin medicus (“physician”).

parole.significato: the price for which a husband acquired authority over a woman
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin meffium, methium, derived from Old High German.
From Medieval Latin merulus (“battlement”). Probably cognate with French and English merlon, Spanish merlón.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin metaphysica, from Ancient Greek μετὰ τὰ φυσικά (metà tà phusiká, literally “after that which is natural”).

parole.significato: Attribute to Saint Anne, when depicted as third behind the Virgin Mary with Christ child on her lap.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mettertia, from -met (intensifying particle) + tertia (“third”, whence Italian terza).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin miliāris.
From Medieval Latin miraculosus, or from miracolo + -oso.

parole.significato: bilberry, whortleberry, blueberry, bearberry, cranberry, lingonberry, cowberry, huckleberry; a plant of the genus Vacci…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin myrtillus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin misericordiōsus.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin morganaticus (possibly via French morganatique), from Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō (“morning-gift”) (compare Old High German morgangeba), from *murginaz (“morning”) + *gēbǭ (“gift”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin musaicum, from Late Latin musivum (opus), from Latin museum, musaeum, probably from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses, (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)).
From Medieval Latin movibilis.
From muovere + -mento, perhaps based partly on Medieval Latin mōvimentum, from Latin moveō. Compare French mouvement.

Likely from Medieval Latin muffula (817, Carolingian), a Germanic borrowing from Frankish *molfell (“soft garment made of hide”), from *mol (“softened, forworn”) + *fell (“hide, skin”), from Proto-Germanic *mildijaz (“tender, soft”) + *fellą (“skin, film, fleece”). Compare modern Dutch moffel.
From Medieval Latin mumia, from Arabic مُومِيَاء (mūmiyāʔ), from Persian مومیا (mumyâ), from موم (mum, “wax”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin mundoaldus, of Germanic origin.
From muscolo (“muscle”) + -are, or borrowed from Medieval Latin musculāris.
From Medieval Latin mūsicālis, derived from Latin mūsica.
From Medieval Latin nadir, from Arabic نَظِير السَّمْت (naẓīr as-samt), composed of نَظِير (naẓīr, “counterpart, corresponding to”) and السَّمْت (as-samt, “the zenith”).
From Medieval Latin necrologium.
From Medieval Latin nenuphar, from Arabic نِلُوفَر (nilūfar), نِينُوفَر (nīnūfar), from Middle Persian nylw(k)pl (nīlōpal, “lotus, water-lily”), from Sanskrit नीलोत्पल (nīlotpala, “blue lotus”).
From Medieval Latin nocibilis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin nocumentum.
From Medieval Latin nonagium, derived from Classical Latin nōnus (“ninth”).
From Medieval Latin and Late Latin notōrius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin nubifragium, from nūbēs (“cloud”) and frangĕre (“to break”) (by analogy with naufragium (“shipwreck”)).
From Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ).
From Medieval Latin numerus Arabicus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin obiectīvus.
From Medieval Latin ōceanicus, from Latin ōceanus. By surface analysis, oceano + -ico.
From Medieval Latin offēnsīvus, from Latin offēnsus, past participle of offendō (“to offend”) (compare offenso).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin obiectum.
From Medieval Latin omniscientem. By surface analysis, onni- (“omni-”) + sciente (“aware, conscious”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin omniscientia. By surface analysis, onni- + scienza.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin organizāre (“to organize”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin opticus, from Ancient Greek ὀπτικός (optikós, “of seeing”).
From Medieval Latin ovālis.

From Medieval Latin balla, palla, bala, from Frankish *ballu, from Proto-Germanic *balluz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoln- (“bubble”), from *bʰel- (“to blow, swell, inflate”). Alternatively, via Lombardic *palla, from Proto-Germanic *ballô, from the same ultimate origin. Compare Sicilian baḍḍa.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin parafernālis, paraphernālis, derived from Latin parapherna.
From Medieval Latin parochus (“parish priest”). Cognate with Sicilian pàrrucu.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin partītīvus, from Latin partītus + -īvus.
From Medieval Latin paternālis, from Latin paternō (from which the cognate paterno).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin petroleum.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pilotus, alteration of Latin pedota, from Ancient Greek πηδόν (pēdón, “oar”), from πούς (poús, “foot, leg”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin plica, a derivative of Classical Latin plicō (“to fold, bend or flex; roll up”). Compare Sicilian chica. Doublet of piega.
From Medieval Latin polāris.
From Medieval Latin apodissa (“receipt for money”), from a Byzantine Greek *ἀπόδειξα (*apódeixa), from Ancient Greek ἀπόδειξις (apódeixis, “proof”). Doublet of the learned borrowing apodissi.
Dissimilation from earlier porfiro, from Medieval Latin porphyrium /porphyrum, from Latin porphyrītēs.

parole.significato: portolan (chart of European navigable waters based on descriptions of coasts)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin portulānus, derived from portus (“harbour/harbor, port”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin postcommūniō, derived from Classical Latin post (“after”) + commūniō (“communion”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin postilla, from post illa (verba) "after those words".

parole.significato: to put into practise/practice, to implement
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prāctica (“practical affairs, business”), from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτική (prāktikḗ, “practice, experience”), from πρᾱκτικός (prāktikós, “practical”), from πρᾱ́σσω (prā́ssō, “I do”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from Late Latin praeambulō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin praecōnizāre, derived from Latin praecōnium (“publishing, proclaiming”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin praedicāmentum, derived from Latin praedicō (“to declare, proclame, predicate”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin praedīligere (“to esteem before others”), from prae- (“before”) + dis- (“apart; utterly”) + legere (“to choose”). By surface analysis, pre- + diligere.
From Medieval Latin praeferentia.
From Medieval Latin praelātus.
From Medieval Latin prīmōgenitūra.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin priōritātem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōiectilis (“projectile”), from Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth; extend; expel”). By surface analysis, proietto + -ile.
From Medieval Latin, Vulgar Latin promissa (“promise”), from Latin prōmissum (“promise”), from promittō (“to send forth; to promise”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin prŏgnōsticāre, from prognōsticus, from Ancient Greek προγνωστικός (prognōstikós, “foreknowing”), from προ- (pro-) + γνωστικός (gnōstikós, “of or for knowing, good at knowing”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to learn to know, to perceive, to mark, to learn”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin propīna, from prōpīnāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōpulsiōnem, from Latin propulsus.
From Medieval Latin prostata, from Ancient Greek προστάτης (prostátēs, “one standing before, protector”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōtocollum, from Byzantine Greek πρωτόκολλον (prōtókollon, “first sheet glued onto a manuscript”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”) + κόλλα (kólla, “glue”).

parole.significato: synonym of scamorza: scamorza (an unfermented cow's-milk cheese from southern Italy)
parole.testo: From provare or from Medieval Latin probula (compare Latin būbalus (“buffalo”)). Far from old central Italian linguistic theories, perhaps it would be more practical to reason about the Italianization of the Sicilian term prùvula.
From Medieval Latin quālificātiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin quidditātem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin quiētūdinem.
From Medieval Latin quindena (“quindene”), from Latin quindeni (“15 each”), owing to the Roman and medieval practice of counting inclusively.
Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin quodlibet, from Latin quod libet (literally “that which is pleasing”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin quotātiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rāmificāre (“to branch, ramify”), from Latin rāmus (“a branch”) + faciō (“do, make”).
Ultimately from Medieval Latin rapuntium from Latin rapunculus, diminutive of rapum (“turnip”). By surface analysis, rapa (“turnip”) + -onzolo.
From Medieval Latin rata, from the Latin phrase pro rata parte (“according to the proportional share”), from ratus (“reckoned”), past participle of the verb reor (“to think over, deem, reckon”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ratificāre, from Latin ratus (“established, authoritative; fixed, certain”) + faciō (“to make”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin reālitātem, from Late Latin reālis (“real”), from Classical Latin rēs (“thing”) + -ālis. Doublet of realità, which is a learned borrowing.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rēgālia, “gratuity” sense influenced by regalare.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin relevium, derived from Classical Latin relevō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus.
From Medieval Latin residentia, from Latin residēns (“residing”), from resideō (“to reside”), from re- + sedeō (“to sit”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin retentīvus, from Latin retentus. Doublet of ritentivo.
From Medieval Latin ribes (“currant”), from Arabic رِيبَاس (rībās, “Syrian rhubarb; currant”), from Persian ریواس (rivâs, “rhubarb”), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *(h)rabā́š (“rhubarb; fennel”).
From Medieval Latin receptivus, from Latin receptus.
From riflesso + -ivo, or from Medieval Latin reflexīvus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus.
From Medieval Latin retentīvus, from Latin retentus. Doublet of retentivo.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin retorsiōnem, derived from retorsus, alternative form of Latin retortus, perfect passive participle of retorqueō.

parole.significato: rochet (garment worn over the choir cassock by cardinals, bishops and certain other dignitaries)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin roccus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rotātōrius, from Classical Latin rotō. Cognate with Catalan rotatori, French rotatoire, Portuguese rotatório.
From Medieval Latin rotulāre (“to roll, revolve”), from Latin rotula (“a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (“a wheel”). Doublet of rullare.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rubīnus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin saphena, from Arabic صَافِن (ṣāfin), from Hebrew צֹפֵן (ṣōfēn, “hiding”).

parole.significato: the raft that supports a floating mill on a river
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin sandones.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the House of Della Scala, an influential Veronese family.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Scaliger (literally “ladder bearing”, from scala + -ger), a Latinization of Della Scala, the name of the family that ruled Verona in the 13th and 14th centuries.

parole.significato: scapular (short cloak worn around the shoulders by Benedectine monks)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin scapulāre, from Latin scapula.
From Medieval Latin scarlātum (“scarlet cloth”), from Persian سقرلات (saqerlât, “a warm woollen cloth”).
From Medieval Latin siruppus, syrupus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”).
From Medieval Latin sclareia.
From Medieval Latin scōpīlia (“sweepings, refuse”). Cognate with Neapolitan scupiglia.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin scrīptōrium (“writing desk; writing room”), derived from Classical Latin scrīptus (“written”), perfect passive participle of scrībō (“to write”). Doublet of scrittoio.

parole.significato: the office of a Lombard steward; their jurisdiction
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin sculdasia, derived from sculdasius.

parole.significato: a Lombard steward of a duke who had both civil and military authority
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin sculdasius, sculdachius, from Lombardic *skuldhaizio.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sebesten, from Arabic سِبِسْتَان (sibistān), from Persian سگپستان (sag-pestân, literally “dog teat”), from سگ (sag, “dog”) + پستان (pestân, “teat”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sēdātivus, from Latin sēdātus, perfect passive participle of sēdō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius, from Latin sēcrētus. By surface analysis, segreto (“secret”) + -ario (“-ary”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin simplificārī.
From Medieval Latin seraphicus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin serpīginēs.
From Medieval Latin simultāneus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin siniscalcus, from Proto-Germanic *siniz (“old”) + *skalkaz (“knight, servant”).
From Medieval Latin Sina (“China”), from Latin Sinae (“the Southern Chinese; Southern China”), from Ancient Greek Σῖναι (Sînai), q.v. Doublet of cino-.
From Medieval Latin syringa, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pipe, syrinx”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Slavus, from Late Latin Sclāvus, from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos), which see for more. See also the related term schiavo.
Ultimately from Medieval Latin smaltum, likely via some Gallo-Romance language (in particular Old Occitan esmalt).

parole.significato: a unit of fluid measure used in Mantua and Modena, where it was equivalent to approximately 109.36 litres and 50.9 litr…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin solium, from a development of Latin solium (“tub, bathtub”).
From Medieval Latin sortilegium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin subterfugium, from Latin subterfugiō (“to flee secretly”), from subter (“under”) and fugio (“to flee”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin stantīvus. By surface analysis, stante + -io.
From Medieval Latin stigmatizō, from Byzantine Greek στιγματίζω (stigmatízō). By surface analysis, stigma + -izzare.
From a conflation of Medieval Latin usitilia (“a storing place”) and usibilia (“usable things”).
From Medieval Latin stupha, perhaps ultimately from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos, “smoke, steam”), from τύφω (túphō, “to smoke”). Same as English stew.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin superiōritātem, derived from Latin superior. By surface analysis, superiore + -ità.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin tac(c)uinum, from Arabic تَقْوِيم (taqwīm, “calendar”). Compare Venetan tacuin.
From Medieval Latin tamisium, probably from Gaulish. Compare French tamis.
From Medieval Latin tannō, from Late Latin tannum (“oak bark”), probably of Celtic origin, from Gaulish *tannos (“oak”), from Proto-Celtic *tannos (“green oak”).
From Medieval Latin tara, from Arabic طَرْح (ṭarḥ, “rubbish, refuse”), from طَرَحَ (ṭaraḥa, “reject, deduct”).
From Medieval Latin thaumaturgus, from Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós).

parole.significato: to play for time; to temporize
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin temporizāre, from Latin tempus (“time”); adapted to the suffix -eggiare.
From Medieval Latin tendō (“tendon”).

parole.significato: terra sigillata (type of fine, red Roman pottery)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin terra sigillāta (literally “sealed, stamped earth”).
From Medieval Latin tiburium, perhaps an alteration of cibōrium.
From Medieval Latin or Late Latin timorōsus, from Latin timor; probably altered from the older form temoroso, now obsolete. Compare Catalan and Occitan temorós, Portuguese and Spanish temeroso.
From Medieval Latin thōrācicus, from Ancient Greek θωρᾱκικός (thōrākikós).
From Medieval Latin tōtālis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānsubstantiāre.
From transustanziare, from Medieval Latin trānsubstantiāre. By surface analysis, transustanziar(e) (“to transubstantiate”) + -si (“oneself”, enclitic reflexive pronoun).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānsubstantiātiōnem.
From Medieval Latin trānspārentem (“transparent”), present participle of trānspareō, from Latin trāns + pareō.

parole.significato: to transpire (of liquids exuded through pores in plants or animals)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspīrāre, from Latin trāns + spīrō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspīrātiōnem, from trānspīrō, from Latin trāns + spīrō.
From Medieval Latin triforium.
From Medieval Latin *trottāre, *trotāre (“to go”), from Frankish *trottōn (“to go, run”), from Proto-Germanic *trudōną, *trudaną, *tradjaną (“to go, step, tread”).

parole.significato: uxoricide (the killing of one's own wife)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin uxoricīdium.
From Medieval Latin valesius, of uncertain origin.

From Medieval Latin vāna glōria, from Latin vāna (“empty, groundless, boastful”) + glōria (“fame, ambition, boasting”). By surface analysis, vana (“vain”) + gloria (“glory”). Cognate with English vainglory, Portuguese vanglória and Spanish vanagloria.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin vapōrābilis.
From Medieval Latin vegetālis, from Latin vegetō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin velleitātem, from Latin velle (“wish, will”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin vērācitātem.

From Medieval Latin vernix, from Latin veronix, from Byzantine Greek βερενίκη, βερονίκη (bereníkē, beroníkē, “resin amber”), from Ancient Greek βερενίκιον, βερονίκιον (bereníkion, beroníkion, “soda”), from Βερενίκη (Bereníkē). Cognate with Piedmontese vernis/vërnis.
From Medieval Latin versiōnem.
From Medieval Latin vitrōsus.
From Medieval Latin vimpa, from Frankish *wimpil, *wimpila (“head scarf”), from Proto-Germanic *wimpilaz, from Proto-Germanic *wīpaną (“to wind, swing”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin vīsīvus, derived from Classical Latin vīsus. Cognate with Piedmontese visiv.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin volitivus, from volitiō (compare volizione), from Latin volō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin volitiōnem, based on Latin volō (“to want”).
From Medieval Latin cenit, a transliteration of Arabic سَمْت (samt, “direction, path”) which is in itself a weak abbreviation of سَمْت الرَأْس (samt ar-raʔs, “direction of the head”).
From Medieval Latin zibethus, from Arabic زَبَاد (zabād).

parole.significato: to besiege, to lay siege to
parole.testo: Perhaps a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin assediāre, reshaping of Classical Latin obsidēre. Alternatively, derived from assedio (“siege”) + -are (1ˢᵗ-conjugation verbal suffix).

From Medieval Latin bombacium, Byzantine Greek βαμβάκιον (bambákion), from either Ancient Greek βάμβαξ (bámbax, “cotton”) or Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux, “silk-worm”), whose ultimate origin is unknown. Compare Greek βαμβάκι (vamváki), Venetan bonbaxo, Middle Persian pmbk' (pambag).
Borrowed from Spanish caramelo or French caramel, from Portuguese caramelo, itself either from Late Latin calamellus, or Medieval Latin cannamellis.

From Medieval Latin or Late Latin dentālis, derived from Latin dēns (“tooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts. By surface analysis, dent(e) (“tooth”) + -ale (“-al”, adjectival derivational suffix).

From the feminine of the past participle of offrire, or from Medieval Latin or Late Latin offerta, ultimately from Latin offerō. Compare Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan, and Sardinian oferta; Friulian ufierte; Romansh offerta; Sicilian ufferta.

Borrowed from Old French estival, of which the etymology is disputed: either from Medieval Latin aestivālis (“summerly”), in place of Classical Latin aestīvus (whence also Italian estivo), from aestās (“summer”), or from tībiālis (“tibial, of the tibia”), from tībia. Cognate with Sicilian stivala.

Borrowed from a language of Northern Italy (cf. Venetan valís, Lombard valiza), from Medieval Latin valesia, valixia, from Late Latin valisia, possibly from Gaulish *valisia (“leather bag”), from Proto-Celtic *wal- (“to enclose, surround”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH-. Or, possibly from Arabic و
